key_insight: RL-trained LLM agents can learn to call tools for the wrong reason, using superficial prompt cues instead of actual task need.
engineering_relevance: For reliable agent systems, tool-use policies should be trained and audited against spurious cue dependence, not just raw task success.
method: Built controlled synthetic QA and math environments with cue-to-tool correlations that are causally irrelevant.
Ran counterfactual tests where cues remained but tools were unnecessary to detect shortcut tool invocation.
Added a dense decision-level reward from an LLM judge to score whether each tool call was actually necessary.
evidence_signal: Across counterfactual evaluations, spurious tool invocation rose by up to 39%, and shortcut behavior appeared mainly when the agent already used the target tool reliably.
watch_item: The mitigation depends on an LLM judge for tool-necessity scoring, which may introduce extra cost and its own evaluation bias.
paper_title: Spurious Tool Use: When RL Agents Learn the Wrong Reason to Act
